## Scope and development status

This draft follows the recommended 90-minute programme below, replacing the
earlier two-hour format. Dataset documentation and FAIR metadata are core
activities; `synthpop` and `vetiver` are optional extras in the final five-minute
discussion. Installation, production model deployment, and a full treatment of
differential privacy are outside the timed programme.

The [page plan](workshop_pages.qmd) tracks the drafted lessons, the
`HealthWellbeing` pipeline, the report template, and the optional
examples. A timed rehearsal and the prepared participant environment
are pending. The lockfile currently records renv 1.0.7 under R 4.4.1.

Participants should have basic familiarity with R and receive a prepared
project and verified computing environment before the session. The intended
result is one documented workflow with a versioned input, tracked analysis,
reproducible report, and prepared archive record.

## Learning objectives

By the end of the core programme, participants should be able to:

- Explain how Git/GitHub, renv, and Docker support collaboration and reproducibility.
- Document dataset variables, provenance, licensing, and access conditions using
  a codebook and structured metadata that support FAIR principles.
- Store dataset versions with `pins` and retrieve a specified version.
- Trace inputs and outputs through a `targets` pipeline and a Quarto report.
- Identify the materials and metadata needed for an archived, citable release.

Independent model versioning and synthetic-data generation are follow-up options
rather than required participant outcomes.

## Recommended 90-minute workshop programme

| Time | Duration | Topic | Tools |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–5 min | 5 min | Introduction to open and reproducible science | R |
| 5–17 min | 12 min | Version control, collaboration and sharing | Git, GitHub |
| 17–30 min | 13 min | Reproducible computational environments | renv, Docker |
| 30–42 min | 12 min | Dataset documentation and FAIR metadata | codebook, dataspice |
| 42–50 min | 8 min | Dataset storage and versioning | pins |
| 50–68 min | 18 min | Reproducible analytical pipelines | targets |
| 68–80 min | 12 min | Reproducible reporting and publishing | Quarto |
| 80–85 min | 5 min | Research archiving and persistent identifiers | Zenodo |
| 85–90 min | 5 min | Optional extras and concluding discussion | synthpop, vetiver |
| **Total** | **90 min** | | |

### Delivery and pacing

- **0–5 minutes:** introduce the research question and show the prepared project.
  Connect each later step to a reproducibility problem.
- **5–17 minutes:** inspect the repository, make one small change and commit, and
  demonstrate GitHub collaboration and sharing using a prepared example.
- **17–30 minutes:** inspect the lockfile and Docker configuration. Explain R
  package dependencies versus the wider computing environment. Complete full
  dependency restoration and image builds before the session.
- **30–42 minutes:** inspect a prepared `codebook` output, complete a few variable
  descriptions and units, and connect them to `dataspice` metadata for creators,
  access, and dataset description. Discuss findability, accessibility,
  interoperability, and reusability (FAIR), including licence and access conditions.
- **42–50 minutes:** write two small dataset versions to a prepared local `pins`
  board and retrieve an earlier version by its identifier.
- **50–68 minutes:** run a small, scaffolded `targets` pipeline, inspect its
  dependency graph, change one input, and observe which outputs need rebuilding.
- **68–80 minutes:** render a prepared Quarto report from the pipeline outputs,
  inspect provenance, and show a prepared publishing example rather than requiring
  every participant to deploy a site.
- **80–85 minutes:** inspect a prepared Zenodo deposit and its citation metadata.
  Explain persistent identifiers and versioned releases without requiring live
  publication by participants.
- **85–90 minutes:** briefly signpost `synthpop` and `vetiver`, using prepared
  outputs if time permits, then invite questions and identify follow-up resources.

Use one small participant action per segment and supply completed checkpoints
and example outputs for anyone who falls behind. Each allocation includes its
explanation, activity, and transition; there is no separate setup buffer. Keep
concluding discussion even if optional demonstrations are skipped. Dates, venues,
and announced session details belong in [announcements](../ANNOUNCEMENTS.md).

## Proposed revised abstract

Open and reproducible science helps research be understood, evaluated, reused,
and extended by others. This 90-minute workshop introduces a practical research
workflow using R and open-source tools.

Participants will follow one prepared project through version control and
collaboration with Git and GitHub, reproducible environments with renv and
Docker, and dataset documentation using codebook and dataspice. They will explore
how variable descriptions, provenance, licensing, and access metadata support
FAIR research data.

The workflow connects dataset storage and versioning with pins to analytical
pipelines with targets and reproducible reporting and publishing with Quarto.
A short Zenodo demonstration introduces archiving and persistent identifiers.
Optional closing examples signpost synthetic data with synthpop and model
versioning with vetiver.

The emphasis is on transparent, portable, auditable, reusable, and accessible
research, with clear documentation of limits on data access and reuse. Activities
use public teaching data and prepared scaffolding so participants can focus on
the connections between the tools.

## One practical research project

Use the publicly accessible `HealthWellbeing` teaching dataset and
pool the study correlations. Preserve the raw file and explain
cleaning, missing-value checks, and modelling assumptions. Check
upstream reuse terms before adding data to an archive.
[Section 4.2.4, Correlations](https://doing-meta.guide/pooling-es#correlations)

1. **Track the project and environment.** Provide a Git repository containing
   analysis helpers, metadata templates, a lockfile, and Docker configuration.
   Participants inspect the prepared files and record a small change.
2. **Document the dataset.** Use `codebook` to inspect variable descriptions and
   summaries, and `dataspice` to prepare structured dataset metadata. Record the
   source, creators, licence, access conditions, units, and processing decisions.
   These tools support FAIR practices; using them does not by itself establish
   that a dataset meets every FAIR principle.
3. **Store and retrieve versions.** Prepare a local `pins` board with versioning
   explicitly enabled. Write two dataset versions and retrieve a specified
   earlier version. Keep metadata linked to the matching data version.
4. **Run the analytical pipeline.** Use `targets` to connect the selected dataset
   version, preparation, a simple analysis or model, and output files. Make the
   version identifier an explicit input rather than silently reading whichever
   version is newest. Supply short-running targets and completed checkpoints.
5. **Report and publish.** Use Quarto to read the tracked output files and explain
   methods and results. Record the dataset version, code revision, analytical
   settings, and environment information needed to trace each result.
6. **Prepare an archive.** Assemble code, documentation, permitted data, and the
   report for a GitHub release and a prepared Zenodo deposit. Inspect authorship,
   licensing, version information, and the persistent identifier.

Optional closing examples can reuse the dataset and any simple fitted model.
Neither synthetic-data generation nor separate model storage is required to
complete the core workflow.

## Tools and scope

| Tool | Planned teaching role | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [R](https://www.r-project.org/) | Shared language and prepared project | Core introduction |
| [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [GitHub](https://github.com/) | Change history, collaboration, and sharing | Core, 12 minutes |
| [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/), [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) | R dependencies and the wider computing environment | Core, 13 minutes; setup completed beforehand |
| [codebook](https://cran.r-project.org/package=codebook) | Variable descriptions, labelled missing values, and summaries | Core metadata segment, shared 12 minutes |
| [dataspice](https://docs.ropensci.org/dataspice/) | Structured metadata using CSV templates and Schema.org descriptions | Core metadata segment, shared 12 minutes |
| [pins](https://pins.rstudio.com/articles/pins.html) | Dataset storage, version identifiers, and historical retrieval | Core, 8 minutes |
| [targets](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) | Analysis dependencies, tracked outputs, and selective rebuilding | Core, 18 minutes |
| [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) | Reproducible reporting and publishing | Core, 12 minutes |
| [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) | Archiving and persistent identifiers | Core demonstration, 5 minutes |
| [synthpop](https://www.synthpop.org.uk/) | Synthetic-data illustration and limits on interpretation and sharing | Optional closing example within the final 5 minutes |
| [vetiver](https://vetiver.posit.co/get-started/version.html) | Model storage, input requirements, and prediction dependencies | Optional closing example within the final 5 minutes |

`pins` and `vetiver` support versioned storage, but project-specific provenance
links still need to be supplied as metadata. Enable versioning explicitly for a
local folder board. Capture the computational package environment with `renv`
alongside the model's prediction dependencies.

Test the chosen package versions together before adding them to the workshop
lockfile. Prepare `codebook` output and partially completed `dataspice` templates
in advance so the metadata activity fits its time allocation.

## Optional extras and responsible sharing

The final five minutes combine optional examples with concluding discussion;
they are not two additional practical exercises. Use prepared outputs and
provide fuller material for follow-up.

- **synthpop:** show a synthetic version of the public teaching data and one
  comparison with the original. A runnable synthetic-data workflow does not let
  others verify findings computed from inaccessible originals. Ordinary synthesis
  with `synthpop` must not be presented as a differential privacy guarantee;
  utility or disclosure-risk scores do not establish one.
- **vetiver:** show a prepared model record with its dataset version, code
  revision, settings, input requirements, and prediction dependencies. Creating
  a model API or deploying a service is follow-up work.

Versioning and metadata do not automatically make a dataset or fitted model
appropriate for public release. A model trained on restricted data can reveal
sensitive information, and synthetic data does not confer privacy protection
on related models, evaluation results, or metadata.

A fuller differential privacy extension, if developed later, needs a separate
review of its mechanism, assumptions, privacy accounting, and randomness before
any guarantee is claimed. It is outside the timed programme.

Background: [NIST's synthetic-data overview](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/cybersecurity-insights/differentially-private-synthetic-data)
and [guidelines for evaluating differential privacy guarantees](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/226/final).

## Development work

- Review the dataset documentation, analysis assumptions, and reuse terms.
- Prepare the Git/GitHub activity and verify the participant environment before
  the session, including the required dependencies under R 4.4.1.
- Prepare a `codebook` output and partially completed `dataspice` templates with
  source, licence, access, and variable metadata for the 12-minute activity.
- Build the eight-minute `pins` exercise with two versions and explicit
  historical retrieval, preserving raw data.
- Implement the short-running `targets` pipeline, dependency graph, and
  selective-rebuild activity for the 18-minute segment.
- Prepare the Quarto report, publishing example, and provenance fields.
- Prepare a permitted archive example and citation metadata for the five-minute
  Zenodo demonstration.
- Test package versions before recording them in `renv.lock` and rebuilding the
  workshop environment; do not treat current placeholders as working examples.
- Prepare optional `synthpop` and `vetiver` outputs and follow-up resources, with
  reproducible seeds for ordinary stochastic teaching examples and clear limits
  on privacy claims.
- Rehearse the exact 90-minute sequence, including transitions, checkpoints,
  fallback outputs, and concluding discussion.
